newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian banks hail free interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian banks hail free interest rates.

text.p: Nigerian banks on Wednesday welcomed the military government's decision to abolish interest rate ceilings and allocation of credit, but said adjustments had already been made.
"These moves had been expected by the end of this financial year with or without World Bank pressure, so we had already adjusted," Tony Onwu, of FSB International Bank told Reuters.

Shunned by most western countries for human rights abuses and lack of democracy, heavily indebted Nigeria has been under pressure from the World Bank and International Monetary Fund to abolish restrictive economic policies.

Finance Minister Anthony Ani, at the World Bank and IMF meeting in Washington on Tuesday, said a 21 percent ceiling on interest rates had been lifted. At the same time the government ended its system of allocating credits.
"Sectoral allocation of credit meant we had to lend a certain amount to sectors which are essentially loss-making like agriculture," said Onwu.
Latest figures from the government statistics office show annual inflation falling below 30 percent in June.
But banks are already fighting each other to negotiate loans at between 13 and 21 percent depending on the client's risk. Deposit rates are as low as 10 percent.
"Purchasing power is very weak, so companies are just borrowing to meet immediate requirements and paying back straight away. There is a war on to lend to the AAA rating companies," said one banker.

This trend has been fuelled by the injection of cash from the government's Petroleum Trust Fund, set up in 1994 to cushion the blow of a four-fold rise in fuel prices through spending targeted at infrastructure.
"If the government is able to maintain tight liquidity they should keep interest rates within their current band," another banker said.

"Freeing interest rates is an absolutely positive development which makes it easier to operate. At the moment we are just looking at short-term lending, but in the future we will certainly be looking longer term."
Central bank governor Paul Ogwuma said Nigeria's economy was robust enough to ensure interest rates would not soar as they did last time the government tried to end the rate cap.
The IMF and World Bank have been pressing Nigeria, which relies almost entirely on oil revenue, to reform its economy.
Ani said he was also looking at ending the dual currency system where the official rate makes the naira four times more expensive than the market is prepared to pay.
Military ruler General Sani Abacha on Tuesday created six more states, the next step in his plan to return Nigeria to democracy by October 1998.

At the weekend the 53-member Commonwealth, which suspended Nigeria for executing nine minority rights activists in November, said it would not impose sanctions to force the pase of democracy and would try dialogue instead.
